messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

James Sullivan, a 46‑year‑old graphic designer with a calm, methodical habit, had never imagined his life would be punctuated by the flashing blue of a police cruiser. On a rainy Thursday evening in late October, while he was walking home from a late client deadline, a police officer stopped him at a crosswalk that had, according to James’s memory, been empty for months. The officer demanded that James pull over, but James, certain that he had been following the streetlights, stepped off the curb and began to walk, his hand instinctively reaching for the envelope of a design file tucked into his jacket. The officer’s knuckles pressed on the car door, his face turned from confusion to anger, and before James could even ask why he was being stopped, a hand shoved his shoulder, a sharp hiss of rubber, and a sudden, painful sting as a hand struck his face. The officer’s boots, with their dark, scuffed soles, seemed to echo the harshness of the moment. He felt a rush of fear, the kind that makes the heart pound and the vision blur, and when the siren’s wail faded into a distant drone, he was left alone on the pavement, clutching a broken smartphone screen, bruised in places he could not immediately name. From that night forward, James’s world narrowed to the images and sounds that had defined his trauma. The intrusive thought of a police officer’s glare came unbidden when he passed a courthouse, the sight of a child with a torn sleeve on a school bus triggered an immediate recollection of a hand slamming against his own arm, and the very presence of an authority figure—any uniformed person—caused his chest to tighten. These triggers did not simply remind him of the event; they lit a fire in his mind, generating a state of threat. He could not relax, no matter how far from the scene he was, and he constantly mapped escape routes in his mind before he could feel safe, even at his office. In the dim glow of his studio, with a whiteboard full of color swatches and a monitor displaying client logos, his body stayed taut, fingers on the mouse hovering, the muscles of his neck and shoulders ready to respond to a danger that never truly left. The memory of the assault seeped into his life in waves that overwhelmed him. When the memory returned, James felt so much emotion—anger, fear, humiliation—that he would freeze mid‑sentence, unable to finish explaining what had happened to anyone. He could not clearly describe the officer’s face or the exact force of the shove; the narrative tangled like a knot in his mind, leaving him feeling helpless. The mere thought that someone might not believe his version of events, that the system had failed him, seemed to make the memory even more vivid. James had begun to think that the injustice of the incident was a wound that would never heal; the idea that his life had been destroyed by a single act of violence left him feeling as if every color he ever chose was meaningless. Because of these intrusive triggers and the sense of threat that followed, James turned to maladaptive strategies that he had learned from other stressful moments. He began to spend long hours on his phone, scrolling through memes or playing endless rounds of a puzzle game, to keep his mind occupied and to avoid thinking about the officer’s hand. Whenever he felt a flash of a face or heard a siren, he would immediately pull the device out and dive into a stream of social media content, forcing the brain to stay in the present of the screen rather than the present of the past. He also started to avoid other people, refusing to join colleagues for lunch or to attend team meetings, believing that any group setting might bring up authority figures or strangers who could provoke his memories. These avoidance tactics, while offering temporary relief, only deepened the cycle. The longer he stayed in the safety of his screen, the more the memories resurfaced with intensity, and the more he felt threatened by the world outside his studio. James’s negative appraisals compounded this loop. He came to believe that his life had been irreparably damaged; that the world was a hostile place where people could strike without consequence. These beliefs did not just accompany the threat—they amplified it. When a sudden siren drifted through the office hallway, the sense of impending danger rose, and he felt the same tightness in his shoulders he had felt on that rainy night. The memory of the officer’s hand became a constant reminder that the world was unforgiving, and his attempt to escape through screen time only reinforced the perception that reality was dangerous and that he was powerless to change it. In the months that followed, the maladaptive strategies became habits. When James returned to his work, he found himself scrolling through a game for hours, his laptop screen becoming a refuge. He avoided coworkers, which strained his marriage; his wife, Maria, began to feel neglected and frustrated by his isolation. The constant tension made him anxious, and he began to dread even the sight of a police badge, fearing that a simple stop could trigger a flood of memories. By the time he reached out for help, he was exhausted, his sense of meaning extinguished, and his life seemed to have little hope of recovery. The last spark that brought him to therapy was the realization that he could no longer live on autopilot; each day he woke, he was terrified that a passing siren would snap him back into that dark, violent memory. He was most afraid that the cycle would never break, but he also clung to a fragile hope that a professional might help him untangle the tangled web of his mind and restore even a sliver of peace.
